My expectations were way too high. So many people consider it a “classic”, a “cult film”, an absolute must-watch. And yet, I have to say I’m rather disappointed. I actually fell asleep after 40 minutes. I tried to keep watching, I really did, but making it past the one-hour mark felt like asking too much of me. I love the aesthetics, the colours, the framing and even the costumes. But the dialogue? The very foundation of what supposedly makes this film so iconic? It simply didn’t resonate with me. Perhaps it’s a fucking cool and entertaining film. But is being entertaining really enough to justify its place among cinema's greatest classics? Or have we simply mistaken cultural impact for cinematic greatness? For me. The answer is clear : No.

Could possibly be the most overrated movie I’ve ever watched in my life. I did enjoy the non-linear storytelling in Pulp Fiction. Tarantino constantly rearranged the order of events, which kept the movie interesting for me and curious about what was going to happen next, even without a clear direction. There was always something unexpected around the corner. However, I felt like the movie was missing something throughout. Outside of Samuel L. Jackson’s monologues, which were easily some of the most compelling parts of the film, I struggled to find the deeper substance that would make the story truly satisfying. The dialogue is memorable, the structure is creative, and the movie is undeniably influential, but at times it felt like style was prioritized over substance. I can appreciate what Tarantino accomplished without necessarily agreeing that the movie deserves all the praise it gets. Also….  WHY did Tarantino write himself into the movie just to casually drop the N-word? That definitely felt like a choice he didn’t have to make…😂

I understand that criticising Pulp Fiction is practically a criminal offence in certain corners of Letterboxd, but I genuinely don't understand why it's considered quite so untouchable. Quentin Tarantino is clearly a talented filmmaker, and there's no denying that this film changed the landscape of independent cinema. However, I found myself increasingly frustrated by a film that seems far more interested in demonstrating how clever it is than actually telling an engaging story. The non-linear structure is undoubtedly the film's most recognisable feature, but I don't think rearranging a collection of events automatically makes them more interesting. Some of the individual sequences are entertaining, particularly the interactions between Vincent and Jules, but the overall narrative feels strangely disconnected. I appreciate that the fragmented structure is intentional, yet I never found the resulting experience particularly rewarding. The dialogue is another divisive aspect for me. Tarantino clearly enjoys writing conversations, and occasionally he's exceptionally good at it. But there's a point where interesting dialogue becomes people talking for the sake of talking. Several scenes feel unnecessarily prolonged, as though the screenplay is afraid that the audience might forget how clever its characters are if they stop speaking for thirty seconds. Samuel L. Jackson is excellent, and the film has an undeniable sense of personality. The soundtrack is fantastic, the performances are consistently entertaining, and certain moments are genuinely memorable. However, I found the film's constant attempts to be provocative increasingly tiresome. Violence, profanity and unusual characters are not automatically signs of meaningful storytelling. I also think Tarantino's influence has occasionally worked against the film's reputation. So many filmmakers have borrowed from its style that watching it today doesn't necessarily feel as revolutionary as its historical significance would suggest. Three stars. A film I can appreciate without particularly enjoying. Perhaps the real briefcase was the patience I lost along the way.

That being said, what made this film worth the watch was the casting and dialogue. This movie works so well because of its cast; without them, I don't know if I would have been as drawn in. Something I also liked about this film was its non-linear form of storytelling- it makes the experience of watching this film engaging because you're trying to connect the dots in your head. The biggest standout in this movie is Samuel L. Jackson, especially his monologue at the end of the movie. This is like a quintessential role for him. I also think that John Travolta did a damn good job!
